Tax payable for year = modeled federal + Ontario income tax, including the Ontario health premium, plus OAS recovery tax. Effective tax rate = that tax payable ÷ modeled taxable income. Taxable income excludes the OAS repayment. Both figures include other-income context; “Tax attributable to benefits + investments” includes only their additional tax. Paid-tax columns show whether it was funded by benefits/investments or externally while working. A dash means there is no taxable income. Investment growth excludes savings and living expenses. Working-year investment taxes are reported as paid externally and do not reduce account balances. RRSP-to-RRIF conversion at the end of age 71 is an internal transfer, excluded from cash withdrawals; the first mandatory minimum is at age 72. Registered cash withdrawals reconcile as mandatory RRIF minimum + discretionary cash used for living + tax on those living-cost draws + any registered draw needed to cover investment tax when other accounts are exhausted. Living costs remain inflation-indexed from today. Inflation-adjusted figures use year-end purchasing power. Funded tax due can exceed tax paid if income and assets are exhausted. ¹ RRSP deduction savings are external tax savings and are not reinvested.

TRANSPARENCY, BUILT IN

Know what’s behind your numbers.

This is a deterministic, single-person projection for a resident of Ontario, Canada. All inputs and calculations stay in your browser. Inputs are saved automatically in browser local storage and restored when this same page is reloaded in the same browser profile. This storage does not send cookies or data to a server. Reset clears the saved inputs and restores defaults. Private browsing, cleared site data, moving the HTML file, or browser restrictions may prevent restoration. No external assets or fonts are loaded automatically. Tax research checked October 18, 2026; the tax baseline is 2026.

The order of each year

  1. Your current age represents your age at the beginning of the first modeled year, 2026. All ages are modeled at January 1; whole years are used, including the final planning year.
  2. Pension payments begin at the entered pension start age; CPP and OAS begin at age 65, even if you are still working. All three annual amounts are entered in today’s dollars and multiplied by (1 + inflation)years since 2026 through the final planning year. As an annual planning convention, payments are available at the beginning of each year. From retirement onward they cover living expenses first, then investments fund the remaining need. No retirement expenses are withdrawn before retirement. Expenses follow the same inflation factor.
  3. RRSP converts to RRIF at the end of the year labeled age 71. This internal transfer preserves the registered balance and creates no withdrawal or taxable income; the table reports RRSP and RRIF balances separately. CRA minimum draws begin at modeled age 72, whether retired or still working. Any pension/benefit or mandatory RRIF surplus, after living expenses and the initial tax charge, is reinvested in non-registered assets. Benefits are used for spending first, so the two surplus sources are reported separately.
  4. The remaining balances earn a constant allocation-weighted return. Allocation percentages are fixed return weights; taxable rebalancing trades are not modeled. Before retirement, tax on investment income is paid externally and does not trigger portfolio withdrawals or reduce the entered net savings contributions. During retirement, year-end investment tax is paid from the non-registered account first; the remaining selected account order is used only if needed.
  5. Fixed nominal savings for each account are deposited at year-end until the year before retirement. RRSP savings after age 71 are redirected to non-registered assets.

Withdrawal priority and coloured periods

Discretionary withdrawals use your selected account priority, moving to the next account only when the earlier account cannot cover the remaining net cash need. Withdrawals are grossed up for the additional tax they create. Retirement-year investment tax uses the non-registered account first, then the other accounts in your selected order. Before retirement, no discretionary portfolio withdrawals occur; investment taxes are paid externally. Required RRIF minimums from age 72 are the legal exception if retirement is later. Mandatory RRIF minimums take precedence over the discretionary order; any net surplus is reinvested in non-registered assets. The graph tracks and table badges use actual gross withdrawals recorded for each account, so several accounts can be active in the same year. Year-end balances include all withdrawals, growth, savings and reinvestment.

Three accounts. Three tax treatments.

TFSA Growth and withdrawals are exempt from Canadian income tax. Contributions are not deductible.

RRSP / RRIF Growth is sheltered; the entire withdrawal is ordinary taxable income. Actual progressive tax is used, rather than the withholding rate. RRSP deductions reduce tax-context income; estimated deduction savings are listed separately in the annual table and are not reinvested.

Non-registered The starting cost basis is assumed to equal the entered current balance, so pre-existing unrealized gains or losses are not modeled. Bond return is treated as annual interest. Equity distribution yield is treated as foreign ordinary income, with the remaining equity return as unrealized price appreciation. Distributions are reinvested and increase adjusted cost basis. Sales realize a proportional share of gains or losses. 50% of net gains enters taxable income. Realized losses offset capital gains only and carry forward; no carry-back is modeled. An aggregate cost basis is an approximation for a portfolio of securities.

Reading the projection

The graph and annual table show actual projected year-end account balances, including spending, investment growth, tax payments, savings and RRIF surplus reinvestment. Nominal figures are the dollars projected for that year. Inflation-adjusted figures express the same amounts in today’s purchasing power. RRSP/RRIF withdrawals are taxable when taken; remaining balances stay sheltered.

Effective income tax rate

The displayed effective rate is annual federal plus Ontario income tax and OAS recovery divided by modeled taxable income, after RRSP deductions, capital-loss offsets and the OAS repayment deduction. Taxable income includes the other-income context, pension, CPP, OAS, taxable RRSP/RRIF withdrawals, interest and foreign distributions, and 50% of net realized capital gains, less the modeled OAS repayment. Total payable includes the recovery amount. TFSA withdrawals, returned non-registered principal, and unrealized/sheltered growth are excluded. A dash means there is no taxable income. The rate is derived from progressive tax calculations. Its denominator is taxable income, including taxable withdrawals needed to pay tax; it is not a percentage of living expenses. For example, an RRSP-only Ontario resident age 65, using 2026 rules with no other income, needs approximately $291,226 withdrawn to fund $180,000 of living costs and $111,226 of tax: $111,226 ÷ $291,226 = 38.19%. Future indexation, pension income and other accounts can change these amounts. The tax graph has two tabs: effective tax rate (total payable divided by taxable income) and tax payable amounts (nominal and inflation-adjusted dollars). Both start at retirement. Years without taxable income have no effective rate and appear as gaps, while years with taxable income and no tax show 0%. Tax breakdowns remain in the tooltip, annual table and CSV. Both time-series graphs begin at retirement age and label ages at five-year intervals; every annual value remains plotted and available on hover or tap.

Tax model and practical limits

Tax residency is fixed to Ontario, Canada. Federal and Ontario marginal brackets, basic personal credits, the federal BPA phase-out, Ontario surtax, health premium and basic tax reduction are included. Federal and Ontario age and eligible pension/RRIF credits are included. The entered pension is treated as an eligible lifetime employer pension, including before age 65; CPP and OAS do not qualify for pension income credits. Refundable benefits (including GIS), CPP/EI premiums, AMT, foreign withholding/foreign tax credits, Canadian dividend gross-up/credits, fees, and estate/probate costs are not modeled. Tax estimates may therefore differ from a tax return. Canadian dividend-heavy portfolios require a different distribution model.

Enter pension, CPP and OAS separately from the other-income tax context to avoid double counting. Full living expenses should include costs covered by these three payments. The other-income context is used only for tax brackets; it is not added to your portfolio or used to pay expenses. Enter expenses net of any other income you plan to spend. All income amounts are indexed with your inflation assumption. Benefits are entered by you; contribution history and residency eligibility are not estimated. The model uses constant purchasing power for CPP and OAS, without early/late-start adjustments or an automatic age-75 OAS increase.

OAS recovery tax

The annual repayment is 15% of income above the 2026 threshold of $95,323, capped at that year’s entered OAS payment. The threshold follows your tax-indexing option. The repayment reduces modeled taxable income and is added to total tax payable. The model settles recovery in the same annual cash flow rather than reproducing next July’s withholding schedule. Investment withdrawals can increase recovery and are grossed up accordingly.

Future tax thresholds can be indexed uniformly with your inflation assumption or frozen at 2026 levels. This is a scenario assumption; actual provincial indexation policies differ. Rates remain constant. Personal contribution room is not inferred: verify your TFSA and RRSP room before using the savings inputs. The model does not enforce contribution limits or calculate excess-contribution penalties.

Historical returns, used carefully

The default return assumptions use the 2020 Global Investment Returns Yearbook, published by London Business School: global annualized real equity return of 5.2% and bond return of 2.0% over 1900–2019. The initial nominal returns of 7.304% for equities and 4.04% for bonds are derived as (1 + historical real return) × 1.02 − 1, using 2% inflation. All three rate inputs are editable. Inflation changes the purchasing-power and expense calculations; it does not automatically change your chosen nominal returns. These are global historical benchmarks, not observed nominal CAD returns or forecasts. Currency movements and hedging are not modeled. Overwrite the return boxes to use your own nominal assumptions.

The 2026 UBS Yearbook was also reviewed; its public announcement quotes US asset-class returns, which are not substituted for global defaults here. Constant returns do not capture volatility, sequence-of-returns risk or the probability of success. “Funded” means only that this specific scenario covers the modeled spending.
